analysis.one_liner: Exempts hydraulic fracturing for oil and gas production from federal safe-drinking-water injection rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was referred to and received no vote before Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe Drinking Water Act requires a federal permit, through a program run jointly with the states, before anyone pumps fluids deep underground where they could reach drinking water. This bill would have rewritten the law's definitions so that fluids and sand pumped underground during hydraulic fracturing ('fracking') for oil and gas production, and natural gas stored underground, are not 'underground injection' at all — taking those activities out of that federal permitting system. It would also have handed the EPA sole authority to decide whether any activity that went unregulated before October 1995 could be newly regulated, closing off other paths for those activities to be brought under the rules. The bill was introduced by Sen. Inhofe of Oklahoma and one cosponsor and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing, markups, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers and hydraulic fracturing service companies. Removing fracking fluids from the definition of underground injection means those companies would not need federal permits or face federal oversight when pumping fluids and propping agents (typically water, chemicals, and sand) into wells to crack rock and release oil and gas. Underground natural gas storage operators would also be exempted. The EPA-sole-authority provision would shield any activity not federally regulated before October 11, 1995 from being newly swept into the program — by EPA rule, by state petition, or by court order.

how_it_helps.text: It removes hydraulic fracturing fluids and propping agents used to stimulate oil and gas reservoirs from the Safe Drinking Water Act's definition of underground injection, so those operations fall outside the federal permitting program for underground sources of drinking water.

It also excludes underground injection of natural gas for storage, and gives the EPA Administrator sole authority to decide whether an activity not regulated as underground injection before October 11, 1995 can be regulated under the program — preventing EPA, states, or courts from newly covering such activities.

analysis.who_pays: People who depend on underground sources of drinking water, especially near oil and gas drilling. Fracking fluids and returns are injected into or near formations that can connect to aquifers; with the activity carved out of the Safe Drinking Water Act, federal safeguards and permit conditions would not apply, leaving protection to whatever individual state rules exist. The EPA-authority clause would also lock in that arrangement, because activities unregulated before October 1995 could not be newly regulated by anyone other than the EPA Administrator.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households near drilling relying on groundwater

drawbacks.text: Because the exemption applies to fluids injected underground in drilling areas, any well-bore failures or fractures reaching aquifers would fall outside the federal permit system designed to protect underground sources of drinking water.

The bill would give the EPA Administrator sole authority over whether previously unregulated activities can be regulated at all, removing the ability of states or courts to force such activities into the drinking-water protection program.

Supporters would counter that states already oversaw oil and gas field practices and that federal permitting of fracking injections would duplicate state programs and add cost to domestic oil and gas production; the bill's effect was to settle that question in favor of no federal role rather than weigh it on its merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow entirely to oil and gas producers and service companies, which would avoid federal permitting for fracking injections and gas storage; the cost falls on groundwater protection, since the injection practices most likely to be performed near drinking-water sources would sit outside the federal program. The EPA-authority clause is the most consequential piece: it would not just exempt fracking but freeze the status quo as of 1995 against any future expansion of coverage. Weighed honestly, this is a one-sided carve-out; there is no provision in the bill that compensates or protects the public-side interest it removes from federal oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in March 1999, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe, joined by Sen. Jeff Sessions, introduced the bill on March 25, 1999; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

The bill would have excluded hydraulic fracturing for oil and gas production, and natural gas storage injections, from the Safe Drinking Water Act's definition of underground injection, and given the EPA Administrator sole authority over regulating activities unregulated before October 11, 1995.
No further action was ever taken: the bill sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote for the rest of the 106th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities whose drinking water sits above oil and gas formations: with the bill dead, the EPA retained its existing authority to treat fracking-related injections as underground injection under the Safe Drinking Water Act. Oil and gas producers lost nothing they already had — they simply remained subject to the pre-1995 regulatory status quo — though the industry later secured a comparable exemption in a subsequent Congress through a different bill.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Sessions
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Safe Drinking Water Act
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the referred bill — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators were ever attached to the bill, both Republicans, and it never reached a vote, so no party-line split on the merits can be measured.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and hydraulic fracturing service companies
industries.note: The bill would have freed fracking-related underground injections from the Safe Drinking Water Act's federal permitting program, saving those companies compliance costs. The savings come from a weaker federal backstop for the drinking water of people living near drilling.

Gas storage injections would be expressly excluded from the definition of underground injection, removing federal permit requirements. The stakes here are smaller than for fracking; storage wells are typically in depleted fields with established safeguards.
